frameworks.name: Missing First Diamond
frameworks.definition: A mandatory period of open, exploratory messiness at the start of every brief — asking 'what is really going on?' before any assumption about tools or solutions is made — that precedes both divergent and convergent thinking phases.

frameworks.name: Backward Reasoning (Thinking Backwards)
frameworks.definition: Inverting the standard forward-reasoning mode (data leads to conclusion) to ask instead: 'What would have to be true if we want more people to do X?' — sacrificing clarity for vastly greater surface area of creative opportunity.

frameworks.name: Top-Down vs. Bottom-Up Thinking
frameworks.definition: Top-down thinking imposes legibility from above using available aggregate data and pre-rationalised arguments; bottom-up thinking starts from ground-level observation and asks what data is actually needed, revealing problems invisible to top-down analysis.

claims.text: Rory Sutherland (Ogilvy) argues that roughly 90% of success in business — and most progress in science and pharmaceuticals — is highly messy, non-linear, and non-directional, yet most organisational effort is devoted to pretending otherwise and presenting upwards as though things make far more sense than they really do.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland

numbers.axis: fraction of business/scientific success that is messy vs. structured

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that requiring every organisational action to win an argument in advance gives the finance department an effective veto over every business activity and limits the available solution space by approximately 95%, because ideas that do not quite make sense in advance — which are the source of most genuine innovation — are systematically excluded.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: large organisations where decisions require HR or finance approval before action
claims.mechanism: The requirement to win a logical argument before acting gives veto power to rational gatekeepers, who can only approve ideas legible in advance; this structurally excludes the majority of creative solution space that only makes sense retrospectively.
bounded_by: Does not apply to fields governed by immutable physical laws (e.g. engineering, Newtonian physics) where pre-rationalisation is valid

claims.text: Rory Sutherland claims there are far more good ideas that can be post-rationalised than there are good ideas that can be pre-rationalised, because demanding that something makes complete logical and consistent sense in advance is a massive limitation on creative discovery in complex adaptive systems like markets and human psychology.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: complex adaptive systems — markets, human psychology
not applicable to deterministic systems governed by fixed laws
claims.mechanism: In complex adaptive systems, rules can be rewritten by actors; past data is skewed toward what used to happen and toward fast-moving outcomes, meaning pre-rationalised ideas built on that data systematically miss the creative upside available to backward reasoners.
bounded_by: Newtonian physics and engineering, where pre-rationalisation is appropriate because laws are immutable

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that in any organisation where argument-winning is valued over problem-solving, a structurally perverse incentive exists: a rational decision that fails carries no career penalty, while an imaginative decision that fails destroys the decision-maker's career, so individuals rationally suppress creativity to protect themselves.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.mechanism: Asymmetric accountability — rational decisions are blame-free regardless of outcome; imaginative decisions attract credit-stealing if they succeed and career destruction if they fail — makes irrationality the dominant individual strategy even when creativity would benefit the organisation.

claims.text: Rory Sutherland contends that creative people always present their ideas to rational decision-makers for approval, but rational decision-makers never present their conclusions to creative people for challenge — a complete and unvarying asymmetry that systematically suppresses creative opportunity in organisations.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that the act of aggregating and averaging data to make it legible to senior management destroys precisely what is most valuable about that data — the anomalies and outliers — and produces answers that are wrong and almost inevitably boring, because averaging forces a single solution where multiple correct solutions exist.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.mechanism: Averaging collapses a distribution to its mean, eliminating the outliers that carry the greatest diagnostic and creative value; the resulting single answer both misrepresents reality and forecloses alternative correct ideas that exist at the tails of the distribution.

claims.text: Rory Sutherland, citing Canadian autism researcher quoted by Roger L. Martin, claims that in complex research domains it is the outliers on a scatter plot — not the central cluster — that tell the real story and carry the greatest freight in solving a problem, even though outliers are useless for winning top-down arguments.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: complex problem domains where variance in the population carries signal
bounded_by: Outliers are useless for winning a top-down argument requiring aggregate evidence

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that Jeff Bezos's stated heuristic — when aggregate data and individual anecdotes conflict, the data is usually what is wrong — reflects a principled reason to trust anecdotes: they tend to be about outliers, and outliers are the primary carriers of real-world signal in complex systems.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: complex systems where aggregate data masks tail behaviour

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that efficiency-seeking top-down ideas reliably appear to work in the short term because the hidden costs, systemic damage, and second-order consequences only become visible over a longer time horizon, creating a systematic bias toward over-adopting efficiency measures.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: any system where top-down optimisation is imposed for efficiency
claims.mechanism: Short-term measurement captures the direct gains of efficiency while the ecosystem losses (destroyed diversity, degraded soil, eliminated resilience) accumulate slowly and are not attributed to the original intervention, making reversal politically and analytically difficult.

claims.text: Rory Sutherland claims that in psychology and marketing — unlike in physics or engineering — the opposite of a good idea can itself be another good idea, because multiple correct answers exist simultaneously and backward reasoning expands the solution space beyond the single inarguable answer that forward reasoning produces.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: not applicable to Newtonian physics or engineering where laws are fixed
claims.mechanism: Forward reasoning from a single data set yields one conclusion; backward reasoning from a desired outcome yields multiple distinct pathways, each of which may be valid, because human psychology permits rewriting the rules rather than assuming they are fixed.
bounded_by: Does not apply where physical laws are immutable (engineering, physics)

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that scientific and commercial progress follows a Darwinian rather than Newtonian pattern — most breakthroughs happen accidentally, backwards, and non-linearly (penicillin, Viagra) rather than through sequential pre-planned activity — and that organisations are harming themselves by forcing progress to look Newtonian.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that the no-budget diagnostic phase — asking 'what is really going on?' before selecting any tool or solution — is systematically underfunded in creative and business organisations because no stakeholder has a budget line for solving a problem they do not yet know they have.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: creative and business organisations working under client briefs

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that rebranding and cognitively integrating an existing transport system (London Overground added to the Tube map) can create the equivalent of £20 billion of transport infrastructure value at near-zero cost, by making existing capacity comprehensible and therefore usable.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: existing underused physical infrastructure whose capacity is invisible to users due to cognitive barriers
claims.mechanism: Making something cognitively comprehensible (adding it to a map) shifts user perception from 'does not exist' to 'accessible,' converting latent physical capacity into actual ridership and therefore economic value without constructing anything new.

numbers.axis: infrastructure investment required for equivalent passenger capacity gain

anchors.region: London Overground rebrand and Tube map integration

bounded_by: Only applicable where existing underutilised physical capacity exists but cognitive/perceptual barriers prevent use

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that winning at the emotional or psychological level is a prerequisite for commercial success even when every rational feature decision is correct — citing the Volkswagen cup-holder case where 100,000 rational engineering decisions were optimised but the single emotional purchase trigger was ignored, costing Volkswagen an enormous fine and sales volume in the United States.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: consumer product markets where emotional and habitual cues drive purchase decisions
claims.mechanism: The rational decision-making stack can be flawlessly optimised while the emotional decision at the bottom of the decision tree — the one that actually triggers purchase — is ignored, because the emotional trigger is not legible to top-down data analysis.

claims.text: Rory Sutherland claims that Ford North America's decision to electrify existing beloved brands (Mustang, Bronco, Explorer, F-150, Transit) rather than create new standalone electric brands — driven by customer-upward perspective, not managerial-suite sense-making — produced commercially superior outcomes because it preserved emotional equity and repositioned the value proposition (e.g. F-150 Lightning as power backup, not environmental statement).
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: established consumer brands attempting category transition
claims.mechanism: Customers' emotional attachment to existing brand identities carries more purchase weight than rational category logic; electrifying an existing brand leverages accumulated emotional equity, while a new brand must rebuild that equity from zero.

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that implicit social norm framing — making desired behaviour appear to be what sophisticated peers already do — reduces reactance and achieves compliance more effectively than explicit prohibition or instruction, because explicit rules trigger motivated reasoning about exceptions.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: social settings where peer-norm conformity is valued (e.g. Michelin-starred restaurant)
claims.mechanism: Explicit prohibitions ('no mobile phones') invite motivated reasoning for personal exemptions; framing the desired behaviour as what in-group members naturally do converts compliance from rule-following (resisted) into identity-maintenance (embraced).

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that backward reasoning — asking 'what would have to be true for more people to do X?' rather than reasoning forward from available data — sacrifices argumentative clarity but gains massively greater exposure to creative upside, because it opens the problem space to solutions that have never existed before rather than extrapolating from the past.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: creative and innovation contexts in complex adaptive systems
claims.mechanism: Forward reasoning is constrained to solutions that exist in or can be logically derived from past data; backward reasoning allows the solver to imagine conditions that do not yet exist, accessing a vastly larger creative solution space at the cost of logical inarguability.
bounded_by: Backward reasoning produces solutions that are undefendable in advance, making them politically difficult to fund in argument-driven organisations

claims.text: Rory Sutherland, citing James Watt's invention of the horsepower metric, argues that marketing innovation and product innovation are the same activity: both require reframing the value proposition in terms that are legible to the buyer, not the engineer — translating from technical specification into customer outcome language.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: markets where customers lack technical vocabulary to evaluate product specifications

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that the advertising and creative industry has developed a form of Stockholm syndrome — adopting the rationalist metrics (data accountability, measurability) demanded by their corporate clients instead of asserting that the clients' data is often irrelevant — weakening the creative industry's ability to advocate for psychological and emotional approaches.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: advertising agencies operating in corporate client relationships

claims.text: Rory Sutherland, citing Roger L. Martin, argues that top-down sense-making systematically excludes the customer from strategic decisions because the customer gets aggregated and averaged out of the data that reaches the managerial suite, whereas bottom-up thinking starts from individual customer behaviour and works upward.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.mechanism: Aggregation required to make customer data legible to senior management destroys the individual-level variance (anomalies, outliers, emotional triggers) that drives actual purchase decisions, leaving executives with averages that describe nobody in particular.

examples.text: Rory Sutherland describes 18th-19th century German forestry as a canonical case of top-down efficiency destroying a system. German foresters imposed a monoculture of Norwegian spruce — the fastest-growing timber — planted at equal intervals across large mixed forests to maximise efficiency. Local foresters objected that specific patches were ill-suited, rocky, or had wrong soil density, but were overruled because the plan looked coherent from the top. The result was Waldsterben (forest death): the monoculture was paradise for parasites that prey on spruce; the undergrowth was destroyed; ecosystem diversity that had maintained soil quality was eliminated; and the soil rapidly degraded. The plan worked briefly in the short term — as efficiency-seeking ideas typically do — but caused catastrophic long-run damage that was not visible to those who imposed the original instruction.

Rory Sutherland describes Le Corbusier's plan for Paris — to demolish all existing buildings and reorganise the city into separated zones for work, residential, and retail, viewed from the air — as the architectural equivalent of top-down sense-making that ignores ground-level lived experience. He compares it to Brasilia, which makes perfect sense when viewed from the air but fails as a city because most people do not live in the air. The example illustrates that optimising for legibility from above produces designs that are inarguable in principle and unusable in practice.

Rory Sutherland analyzes the failed John Lewis 'at home' store in Tunbridge Wells retail park using a bottom-up walk-through rather than demographic data. Five concrete problems were invisible to top-down data analysis: (1) the store had its own car park requiring a dedicated journey, preventing impulse visits; (2) the entry signage was positioned after the car park turn, not before it; (3) the car park entry was convenient only for people leaving the retail park, not arriving; (4) the store signage faced the narrowest edge, making the store appear a quarter of its actual size; (5) the name 'at home' caused approximately 60% of local residents to assume it was a furniture store, and since only 5% of people are in the market for furniture at any given time, this branding alone severely suppressed footfall. Each of these problems was discoverable only by going to the location and asking 'what do we need to know?' rather than 'what data do we have?'

Rory Sutherland recounts the UNICEF Crocs distribution story as an example of backward thinking creating a free lunch. A UNICEF worker received a large donation of Crocs shoes for unshod children in parts of Africa. The logical approach was to find children without shoes and distribute Crocs directly. Instead, she distributed them through schools to children on their first day: children who received them went home wearing them, other children asked where the shoes came from, and attendance on subsequent days increased because the Crocs became an incentive to attend. The intervention achieved its primary goal (shoeing unshod children) and simultaneously created a school-attendance habit during the critical first week — the period most predictive of continued attendance — at zero additional cost. Rory Sutherland uses this to illustrate that thinking backwards reveals free lunches invisible to rational forward-planning.

Rory Sutherland describes a Saint-Emilion Michelin-starred restaurant that needed to discourage loud mobile phone calls without alienating customers through explicit prohibition. Rather than posting a 'no mobile phones' sign aimed at arriving diners — which triggers reactance — the restaurant posted a notice ostensibly targeted at departing customers but fully visible to everyone entering. The notice framed phone silence as what their sophisticated clientele naturally do, creating an implicit social norm rather than a stated rule. Arriving diners read it, felt they should conform to what the in-group does, and turned off phones without being told to. Rory Sutherland uses this as evidence that for every logical solution there is a better solution discovered by thinking backwards.

Rory Sutherland describes the film The Big Short as an illustration of the distinction between asking 'what data do we have?' versus 'what data do we need?' Banks in New York had aggregate data showing the mortgage market was healthy. The investors in the film asked what data they needed to understand the real situation, then went to Florida and interviewed individual mortgage holders — including a stripper who held eight mortgages — discovering that the ground reality was a complete disaster invisible to New York aggregate data. The investors who acted on ground-level observations (outliers, anecdotes) rather than aggregated top-down data made the correct call that the entire market missed.

Rory Sutherland describes Volkswagen's US market losses as evidence that winning every rational decision is insufficient if the emotional purchase trigger is missed. Volkswagen's German engineers optimised every rational dimension of the car for the US market — a process Rory Sutherland frames as 'winning 100,000 rational decisions' — but refused to include cup holders, which rank around second or third in American consumers' actual car-purchasing decision tree, above cornering ability. The refusal to include cup holders was a rational engineering decision that missed the emotional and habitual purchase trigger, resulting in massive commercial and regulatory costs in the United States.

Rory Sutherland describes Ford North America's electric vehicle strategy as a case study in bottom-up versus top-down thinking. The managerial-suite solution was to create entirely new electric brands for each vehicle category (SUV, crossover, pickup, subcompact) while preserving petrol brands separately — neat from the top, matching the organisational structure. Roger Martin argued from the customer upward: Ford's five real brand strengths were Mustang, Bronco, Explorer, F-150, and Transit, and it should electrify those directly rather than build new brands. The F-150 Lightning was then positioned not on environmental credentials but on its ability to power a household during a grid outage — relevant to doomsday-prepper and off-grid customers who would not respond to green messaging. The Mustang Mach-E was positioned on Detroit heritage and feel. Both succeeded by starting from customer emotional identity rather than organisational logic.

Rory Sutherland describes his personal experience of having wet trouser legs eight minutes before going on stage as an example that the opposite of a good idea (dry the wet part) can be another good idea (wet everything else). Unable to dry his trousers with a hand dryer in the available time, he went outside into heavy rain and stood in it until his entire outfit was uniformly wet. The audience was confused but the problem — asymmetric wetting — was solved. He uses this as a clean illustration of backward reasoning: starting from the desired outcome (uniform appearance) rather than the obvious solution (remove the water).

Rory Sutherland describes James Watt's invention of the horsepower metric as an act of marketing that was indistinguishable from product innovation. Mine owners in the early industrial era were not interested in boiler temperature or cylinder capacity. By inventing a unit that translated engine output into the number of horses it could replace, Watt made the purchase decision trivially simple: a mine owner who could do the arithmetic (replace 25 horses with one engine) was immediately sold. The metric reframed the value proposition from engineering specification to customer outcome, creating a marketing advantage that has survived unchanged to the present day.

practices.text: Before defining any tool or solution for a problem, run a 'missing first diamond' — a deliberately open, exploratory, messy diagnostic phase that asks 'what is really going on?' without any assumed answer, before divergent or convergent solution work begins.

When analysing a business problem, distinguish between 'what data do we have?' (available data, skewed toward the past) and 'what data do we need?' (ground-truth data that may require field observation, interviews, or novel measurement), and actively pursue the latter.

When writing signage, notices, or social-norm cues intended to change behaviour, frame the desired behaviour as what the in-group or sophisticated peers naturally do, rather than as an explicit prohibition, to avoid triggering motivated reasoning for personal exemptions.

When presenting a creative or marketing solution to a rational gatekeeper, pre-empt the veto by articulating a backward-reasoning question ('what would have to be true for this to work?') rather than asserting a conclusion from data — this makes the imaginative logic visible without requiring it to be pre-provable.

When evaluating why a physical retail location or product is underperforming, conduct a ground-level walk-through to identify perceptual, navigational, and naming failures invisible to aggregate demographic or sales data.
